analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to prove and disclose that mental health coverage is equal to physical health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 18 senators including one Independent, never received a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires health plans to cover mental health and addiction treatment no less generously than physical health care. In practice, plans often impose harder-to-see limits on therapy, psychiatric care, and substance use treatment — like narrower networks or stricter approval rules. This bill would force plans to publicly disclose the analyses showing their mental health rules are comparable, subject them to annual random audits, publish denial rates for mental health versus other claims, and create a toll-free consumer complaint line with a public website portal.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer or individual health coverage who need therapy, psychiatric care, or substance use disorder treatment. They would gain an easier way to see whether their plan is treating mental health claims differently, a single phone number to file complaints, and audits of at least 12 plans per year to check compliance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing mental health or addiction care

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans and insurers to publish annual reports showing their nonquantitative treatment limits on mental health and substance use benefits are no more stringent than on medical and surgical benefits.
Requires three federal agencies to run randomized audits of at least 12 plans per year, plus audits of any plan on complaint.
Requires HHS to collect and report to Congress denial rates and reasons for mental health and substance use claims compared with medical and surgical claims.
Creates a consumer parity unit with a toll-free number and public website portal for complaints, plus timely written responses to consumers and annual reports to Congress.
Requires plans to disclose the plan documents, formulas, and methodologies used to decide benefits, not just summaries.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer-sponsored health plans bear the cost of annual parity analyses, disclosure reports, and audits, and some compliance costs could be passed to premiums. The three agencies bear the cost of running audits and the complaint system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The bill adds no new funding line, so the audit, disclosure, and complaint systems depend on agency budgets to work; the minimum of 12 random audits per year is a small share of the plans in the market.
Insurers and employer plans would face real administrative costs for annual parity analyses, reports, and disclosure, some share of which is likely to show up in premiums or employer benefit costs.
The bill relies on disclosure and audit rather than setting benefit levels itself; a plan can comply on paper while still limiting which providers are in network.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — making an existing legal right to equal mental health coverage actually verifiable and enforceable — is broad and reaches millions of people, while the cost is mostly compliance paperwork borne by a concentrated industry. The design is disclosure-and-audit rather than a direct benefit mandate, so its real-world impact depends on agencies doing the audits and acting on findings, and the small audit floor is a fair criticism.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate health committee for the rest of the Congress — the committee never held a markup or vote, and no chamber ever voted on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on May 21, 2019, with 17 original cosponsors — 16 Democrats and Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
The bill received no further action: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House companion vote before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer-sponsored plans are better off because the disclosure, audit, and denial-rate reporting requirements never took effect; consumers gain nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

industries.note: The bill would have required insurers to publish their parity analyses, submit to random audits, and have their mental health denial rates compared with medical denial rates — a direct check on a business practice of applying stricter limits to behavioral health claims.
Employer plans would bear new annual parity analysis, disclosure, and audit obligations under ERISA and the tax code provisions of the bill.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance use treatment providers
industries.note: Stronger parity enforcement means fewer coverage denials and lower barriers for patients seeking therapy, psychiatric care, and addiction treatment, which increases demand for these services.
